title: WHY DOES JESUS POINT BACK TO GENESIS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES JESUS POINT BACK TO GENESIS?

When people tried to pull Jesus into the arguments of His day, He did something startling: He reached past the controversy, past human tradition, and back to the beginning. And what He showed us there still confronts every heart that would rather ask, “What can I get away with?” than, “What did God intend?”
There is a kind of question we ask God when we already know what we want Him to say.
We do not always come looking for truth.
Sometimes we come looking for permission.
Permission to rename what God has already spoken about.
Permission to make Scripture bend around the life we have already decided to live.
And perhaps that is why one moment in the ministry of Jesus feels so painfully modern.
Some Pharisees approached Him with a question about divorce.
“Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?”
It sounds like a theological question.
But Matthew tells us they were testing Him.
This was not merely a wounded person quietly asking Jesus what to do with a shattered marriage. It was a confrontation.
And Jesus could have entered their debate on their terms.
He could have started with their arguments.
He could have begun by cataloguing the competing interpretations surrounding divorce.
Past their attempts to find the boundary line of what was permissible.
Back to the moment before sin fractured the human story.
“Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female...?”
Then Jesus draws directly from Genesis 1:27 and Genesis 2:24.
He does not treat Genesis as disposable religious scenery.
He appeals to creation as authoritative for understanding God’s design.
Because when Jesus was confronted with a question about what humans may do, He pointed His hearers toward what God had done.
When they wanted to discuss permission, Jesus discussed purpose.
When they wanted to know how far something could be broken, Jesus showed them what it looked like before it was broken.
And perhaps that is one reason Genesis matters so much.
Genesis does not merely tell us where humanity came from.
It begins revealing what humanity was made for.
The first subject of Scripture is not you.
Before human governments, cultures, philosophies, algorithms, movements, denominations, arguments, and scandals—
Because if God is Creator, then reality does not begin with what I desire reality to be.
We are creatures before we are commentators.
We receive life before we define life.
We inherit a creation we did not speak into existence.
And Genesis says something breathtaking about the human beings God placed within that creation:
“So God created man in his own image...”
Not in whether somebody wanted you.
Not in whether somebody abandoned you.
Not in whether your father was proud of you.
Not in whether your mother understood you.
Not in the number beside your name on a social-media profile.
Human worth is rooted in something far deeper.
We are creatures made by God, and humanity was uniquely made in His image.
That means the person you despise bears a dignity you did not give them.

It means the unborn, the elderly, the disabled, the poor, the powerful, the forgotten, the stranger, and the person whose life seems completely unlike yours cannot have their fundamental human worth measured merely by convenience or social status.
Your worst chapter is not the author of your value.
But Genesis does not remain in Eden.
Human beings distrust the goodness of God.
Listen to the heartbreaking words of Adam:
“I was afraid... and I hid myself.”
One of humanity’s oldest spiritual reflexes.
We have simply become better at decorating the hiding places.
Some know exactly how to lift their hands during worship while desperately hoping nobody discovers what those same hands were doing in secret.
Some preach grace to everyone except themselves.
Some post Bible verses while their marriage is bleeding behind a locked door.
Some say, “God is good,” because admitting, “I am barely holding on,” feels too dangerous.
We learned to hide a long time ago.
God was not lacking geographical information.
That question still travels through Scripture.
Not where does everybody think you are spiritually?
Not what did you tell your pastor?
Not how many Christian books have you read?
Maybe you are angry with God.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without actually surrendering to Christ.
Maybe everybody calls you strong because nobody has seen you cry in the car before walking into the house.
Maybe there is something on your phone you would panic if your spouse saw.
Maybe you have not prayed sincerely in months.
Maybe you love Jesus, but you are exhausted.
Maybe you failed again last night.
And the instinct inherited from Eden whispers:
Jesus came to destroy the lie that hiding can save you.
This is where understanding why Jesus points back to Genesis becomes bigger than a debate about origins or marriage.
The Bible’s story runs from creation to fall, from promise to fulfillment, from rebellion to redemption, and ultimately toward new creation.
Jesus does not merely remind us what humanity was supposed to be.
He comes to rescue sinners who have become what we were never supposed to become.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help reasonably good people become slightly better versions of themselves.
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
That means your scandal does not surprise Christ.
But neither does His grace give you permission to remain enslaved to it.
Grace is not Jesus standing at a distance saying, “Your sin does not matter.”
The cross tells us simultaneously that sin is more serious than we wanted to admit and that God's love toward sinners is more astonishing than we dared to hope.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ bears judgment for sinners.
And Peter describes what happened with staggering clarity:
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.”
That we might die to sin.
Biblical grace does not say, “Stay hidden.”
It does not say, “Pretend there was never a wound.”
It says, “Bring the wound to the Physician.”
It does not say, “Your choices do not matter.”
It says there is forgiveness so deep that sinners can repent, be cleansed, and learn to walk differently.
And this makes Jesus’ return to Genesis even more beautiful.
When Christ points us toward the beginning, He is not inviting us into nostalgia.
He is revealing God's design in a world distorted by sin.
In Matthew 19, after Jesus points to creation, the Pharisees raise Moses and divorce.
“Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus distinguishes between accommodation to human hardness in a fallen world and God's creational intention.
That principle reaches deeper than marriage.
Surrender searches for the will of the Father.
“How close can I stand to the edge without falling?”
“How close can I walk with Jesus?”
That is a completely different way to live.
And no, this does not mean Christians should weaponize Genesis against wounded people.
Jesus did not commission His followers to become experts at throwing Scripture like stones.
But what our culture calls love can also become cruelty when it requires us to hide truth.
“Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”
This matters especially when talking about marriage, sexuality, identity, human dignity, family, and creation, because these subjects are attached to real people.
Somebody reading this has been divorced.
Somebody stayed and was betrayed anyway.
Somebody carries guilt because they know they were the one who shattered trust.
Somebody grew up watching their parents destroy each other and secretly wonders whether lifelong love is even real.
Somebody is wrestling with desires they never asked to experience.
Somebody is trying to understand what obedience to Jesus will cost them.
Christian truth must never require us to stop seeing the person standing in front of us.
Jesus could look directly at sinners without pretending sin was righteousness.
And sinners could approach Him without discovering that holiness had disappeared.
Consider the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Jesus does not join the mob in destroying her.
Neither does He rename adultery as holiness.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
Jesus refuses our favorite false choice.
We often think we must either condemn people without mercy or affirm everything without discernment.
He loves sinners enough to receive them.
He loves sinners enough to call them out of sin.
And He loves sinners enough to die for them.
This is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is what happens when grace makes hiding unnecessary.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is:

The word carries the idea of changing one’s mind, turning from the former orientation toward a new one. In the biblical call to repentance, this is not merely feeling guilty. It is a genuine turning toward God.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark with:
Fix yourself until God tolerates you.
That is why your story can change.
Not because motivational language is powerful enough.
Not because positive thinking can resurrect a dead heart.
Not because your past suddenly becomes good.
But because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
The Gospel produces new creation in those united to Christ.
And Scripture ends not with God surrendering creation to darkness, but with the promise of renewal.
“Behold, I am making all things new.”
Human rebellion brings exile and death.
The stone cannot keep the Author of life inside.
Death does not get the final word.
Sin does not get the final word.
Shame does not get the final word.
Satan does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
This is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Not because He edits history and pretends your sin never happened.
Not because Christianity offers spiritual amnesia.
Jesus rewrites everything because redemption can give a sinner a future their rebellion could never produce.
Then Peter goes outside and weeps bitterly.
If Peter's failure had been the final chapter, his story would have ended in disgrace.
And later, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus restored the disciple who had denied Him.
Peter was not restored so that denial could become acceptable.
He was restored so that a fallen disciple could follow Jesus again.
Maybe that is what somebody needs to hear tonight.
Get up and run toward Christ.
Stop defending yourself and begin walking in truth.
You think God could never want someone who has done what you have done.
Religious hypocrites who finally humbled themselves.
But do not confuse His welcome with permission to drag your chains into eternity and call them freedom.
Jesus saves us from sin, not merely from embarrassment about sin.
There may be consequences you still have to face.
Forgiveness does not always erase earthly consequences.
Relationships may need years of rebuilding.
Trust may need to be earned.
A confession may cost you something.
Following Christ may dismantle a life you spent years constructing.
But there is a freedom deeper than protecting an image.
There is the freedom of having nothing left to hide from the One who already knows everything.
So why does Jesus point back to Genesis?
Because creation tells us that God—not human appetite—is Creator.
Because Genesis exposes the dignity of humanity and the catastrophe of rebellion.
Because the fracture we experience now makes sense only when we understand that something has gone terribly wrong.
And because the Gospel announces that God has not abandoned His creation to sin and death.
The Bible does not begin with human self-definition.
And your redemption does not begin with you either.
Maybe you clicked this article expecting theology.
And maybe somewhere between Genesis and Calvary, theology found you.
So here is the question you cannot outsource:
Still asking how much of your old life Jesus will allow you to keep?
Still wanting a Savior who forgives you but never a Lord who commands you?
Still performing Christianity while secretly starving for Christ?
You do not need another hiding place.
The Gospel does not promise that repentance will make every earthly consequence disappear.

And if Christ has already carried you from a chapter of scandal into a story of grace, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needs to read tonight.
Send it privately to the person who is ashamed to walk into church.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. The goal is not merely more religious content. It is daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
You cannot glorify God by clicking a button while refusing Him your heart.

Yet Scripture does teach believers to use their resources, voices, generosity, and opportunities for God's glory. So if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ, supporting and sharing it can be one practical expression of stewardship and partnership in spreading biblical truth.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody in your circle may need the Gospel.
If God has given you a voice, use it for His glory.
If He has given you resources, steward them for His glory.
If He has given you a testimony, stop burying it.
If He has given you truth, do not hoard it.
And above everything, if He has given you Christ—
But the Word of our God stands forever.
And when the world keeps asking us to reinvent what it means to be human, Jesus still has the courage to take us back to the beginning.
Perhaps the most haunting question is not whether we have read Genesis.
It is whether we will follow Jesus when He tells us what it means.
The God who found humanity hiding among the trees of Eden is still calling sinners out of hiding—and this time, the road home passes beneath a blood-stained cross and out through an empty tomb.
